newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB futures weaker in thin, technical trade.
newsitem.headline: JGB futures weaker in thin, technical trade.

text.p: Japanese government bond (JGB) futures ended Friday's Tokyo session down in thin, technical trade, traders said.
The outgoing December contract closed down 0.10 at 126.15. The de facto benchmark March contract was down 0.32 at 125.53.
The December has effectively lost its benchmark status as its turnover fell below that of the March.
The turnover of the March was 32,482 contracts, while that of the December was 24,335 contracts.
Liquidation of some option-related longs was behind the JGB futures' fall in mid-afternoon, traders said.

In the JGB futures options market, open interest in the December call option with a strike price of 127.00 was 4,532 contracts -- the largest in the call options market -- as of the close of Thursday. The December options are due to expire on Friday.
Players who were attempting to push December futures towards 127.00 gave up and liquidated longs in the afternoon, traders said.
Also, a Japanese media report saying that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) sees the economy gathering strength triggered some selling, traders said.
"After big gains that followed the BOJ tankan, people were more cautious. A strong rise in housing starts was also used as an excuse to sell," said a brokerage house trader.

The BOJ quarterly "tankan" corporate sentiment survey, released on Wednesday, showed only a limited improvement in business sentiment. Japan's October housing starts, announced earlier on Friday, were up 21.4 percent year-on-year, after an increase of 17.4 percent in September.
Earlier in the afternoon, news that a regional bank in western Japan will hold a news conference triggered some buying, but the impact was short-lived.
Buying quickly waned after a Tottori Bank spokesman said the announcement would not cause worries about Japan's financial system, traders said.
The Osaka Securities Exchange (OSE) later announced that the bank would list its shares on the OSE's second section and on the Hiroshima stock exchange on December 13.
Next week, market participants will be focusing on four-year note auctions, seen likely to take place on December 3, traders said.
"There seems to be good investor demand for four-year notes," said a trader at a city bank's securities unit.
Investors are keen to buy four-year notes before a possible cut in the long-term prime rate, which currently stands at 2.7 percent, traders said.
The Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) customarily sets its long-term prime rate at 0.9 percentage point above its debenture coupon rate.

The yield of the five-year IBJ debenture stood at around 1.65 percent on Friday. If it falls towards 1.60 percent over the next few days, the long-term prime rate may be lowered to a record low of 2.5 percent in December, traders said. -- Kanta Watanabe, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-9780
